s: Part six.
Decomposing complex work.
This is task statement one point six: design task decomposition strategies for complex workflows.
By the end of this part, you'll know when to split work and when to keep it whole, whether to chain steps or discover them, and how to cut the work so nothing falls between the pieces.
Let's start with a picture.
Anyone who has organised a house move knows the calculation.
You can do a job yourself.
Or hand pieces to other people.
Handing out isn't free.
You have to explain what you want.
And for some jobs, the explaining takes longer than the doing.
So what rule do people arrive at?
Split a job when the pieces are genuinely separate, and each can be checked on its own.
Keep it whole when briefing someone costs more than finishing it.
The technical version.
Hold on to this line.
Decomposition buys isolation, and costs context.
What do you gain?
A fresh window.
A narrower set of tools.
A cheaper model, where the work is cheap.
And a piece that can fail without taking the others down.
What do you pay?
You rebuild, in a prompt, everything the child would otherwise have known.
Plus a return trip through the parent.
The notes put the rule as three signals to split on.
Context volume.
Permission asymmetry.
And verification independence.
One.
Split when a subtask throws off logs or search hits that nobody needs afterwards.
Two.
Split when one part needs write access, and the rest should be read-only.
Three.
Split when each piece has its own pass or fail check.
And when do you keep work whole?
First.
When every intermediate result feeds the next decision.
Second.
When success can only be judged across the whole result.
Third.
When piece two needs piece one's conclusions.
Fourth.
When the work is refine and recheck.
Fifth.
When latency matters, and a fresh subagent's cold start would dominate.
And don't split on the org chart.
Or on file count.
Or because the task merely sounds big.
The first decision the exam tests is whether you know the steps in advance.
In plain words, some work is a checklist.
And some work is a detective story.
A pilot's pre-flight checklist is the same every time, in the same order.
And that's the point.
A detective investigating a burglary can't write the steps in advance.
Each clue decides where to look next.
The technical names are prompt chaining and dynamic decomposition.
Prompt chaining is a fixed sequence of prompts, where each step's output feeds the next.
It's reproducible, and auditable.
Dynamic decomposition lets the agent work out the subtasks as it goes, based on what it finds.
It suits investigations, and open-ended work.
Question one.
Here's the scenario.
An engineering organisation wants two workloads.
The first reviews every merged pull request nightly, against a fixed twelve-item compliance checklist.
Auditors require the same steps, in the same order, each time.
The second investigates intermittent production data corruption.
Its origin is unknown, and may lie in any of several services.
Which approach for each?
Take a second.
The answer.
Prompt chaining for the compliance review.
Dynamic decomposition for the investigation.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: the inverted pairing.
Why?
It gives up reproducibility where auditors demand it.
And it scripts steps where they can't be known.
Wrong: prompt chaining for both, with investigation steps defined from the list of known services.
Why?
Predefined steps go wrong the moment findings diverge.
Wrong: dynamic decomposition for both.
Why?
That gives up the reproducibility auditors require, for no benefit.
This is the same test you met in part two, seen from a different angle.
There, it decided pipeline versus agent.
Here, it decides chain versus dynamic.
In both cases, the question is whether the next step depends on what the last one found.
Hold on to this line.
Known steps, chain them.
Unknown steps, let the agent discover them.
Next, how to cut the work.
Question two.
Here's the scenario.
A privacy review asks which code paths write customer personal data to application logs.
The coordinator splits the repository across eight subagents, by team-owned directory.
Each reports only paths that begin and end inside its own directory.
The combined answer misses most real leaks.
Why?
Because personal data is typically read in one team's module, and logged by a shared logging module owned by another team.
What's the fix?
Take a second.
To learn how a rumour spread through a school, you don't assign one investigator per classroom and ask what happened inside each room.
The rumour travelled between rooms.
You assign someone to follow the rumour.
The answer.
In exam terms, the analysis is cross-cutting.
Splitting it by territory produces partial answers, and nobody positioned to see a flow that crosses a boundary.
So decompose by question, not by territory.
For example, one subagent traces every call into the logging module back to its inputs.
Another lists every personal data field, and everywhere it's read.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: split into sixteen smaller directories.
Why?
More territories means more boundaries.
So even more flows fall between subagents.
Wrong: keep the eight, and add a synthesis subagent.
Why?
Synthesis helps when independent lanes each did their job.
But here, the flows that matter were never traced.
So there's nothing to merge.
Wrong: run the eight sequentially, so each reads the previous report.
Why?
It's slower.
And each still only traces its own directory.
That gives us an important contrast with part two.
In the market research case, adding a synthesis step was right.
Each lane had done complete, independent work.
Only the joining-up was missing.
In the privacy case, adding synthesis is wrong.
The split itself prevented anyone from doing the work.
So ask this.
Did each worker have what it needed to find the answer?
If yes, and the answer spans them, add synthesis.
If no, change how you split.
Hold on to this line.
When the thing you're tracing crosses the lines you would split on, split by question instead.
Next, the loop that should never be split.
Question three.
Here's the scenario.
A documentation tool has a writer subagent and a reviewer subagent.
They pass an API guide back and forth until the reviewer approves.
Each round trip carries the full draft, and the reviewer's notes.
Costs have tripled in a month, as guides grew.
And quality stops improving after the second round.
What's the fix?
Take a second.
An author and an editor in different cities post the whole manuscript back and forth for every change.
They pay more postage each time, and re-read the same pages.
Sitting at one desk for the revisions is cheaper and faster.
The spell check can still be sent out.
The answer.
In exam terms, refine and recheck work should not be split across subagents.
Every round trip rebuilds context the other side had a moment ago.
So cost climbs, while quality plateaus.
Keep revision in one conversation.
And delegate only the pieces that can be checked independently, in one pass.
Such as validating every link.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: add a third arbiter subagent to decide convergence.
Why?
That adds a third context to rebuild each round.
Wrong: cap the exchange at three rounds.
Why?
That bounds cost, but still pays the rebuild every round.
And it may stop before the draft is good.
Wrong: move the reviewer to a larger model.
Why?
That raises the price per round, while the rebuild overhead stays the same.
Hold on to this line.
Keep iterative refinement in one conversation.
Delegate only the one-pass, independently checkable bits.
One more principle to finish this part.
Prefer wide and shallow over deep.
Nesting defaults to three layers below the main agent.
And every layer adds a handoff where context is lost, and a summary where detail is dropped.
That's why setting CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_SUBAGENT_SPAWN_DEPTH to one is a defensible default for production coordinators.
Your workers do the work themselves, instead of passing it further down, past the point where you can see what happened.
That's part six.
If you remember one thing, make it this.
Split on context volume, permission differences, and independent checks.
Chain known steps, and discover unknown ones.
Cut by question, not territory.
Never split a refinement loop.
And go wide, not deep.
Coming up in part seven: sessions, resumption and forking.
